## Derivatives: instruments and markets

A **derivative** is a financial contract whose value derives from an underlying asset, rate, or index. The derivative itself doesn't represent ownership of the underlying — it's a claim referenced to it.

### Basic features

Every derivative has:

**Underlying.** What the contract references — stock, bond, commodity, currency, interest rate, index, credit event, even other derivatives.

**Notional amount.** The size of the contract, used to calculate payoffs. Note: notional is rarely exchanged — it's a reference amount.

**Counterparty.** Two parties to the contract — buyer and seller, or long and short.

**Expiration / maturity.** Most derivatives have an end date (some perpetual exceptions).

**Payoff rule.** How the value is calculated at expiration (or at intermediate points for some).

**Price/value.** Most derivatives have **zero value at initiation** by design (no exchange of cash up front, except for options).

### Categories of derivatives

Two broad families:

**Forward commitments.** Both parties **must** transact at expiration.
- Forwards (OTC, bespoke).
- Futures (exchange-traded, standardised).
- Swaps (series of forwards, often interest rates).

**Contingent claims.** Holder has the **right but not the obligation** to transact.
- Options (calls and puts).
- Credit default swaps (CDS — pays only if credit event).
- Other structured products.

### Forwards vs futures

| Feature | Forwards | Futures |
|---|---|---|
| Market | OTC | Exchange |
| Terms | Customised | Standardised |
| Counterparty risk | High (each party to the other) | Low (clearing house guarantees) |
| Daily settlement | No (settled at maturity) | Yes (mark-to-market daily) |
| Margin | Bilateral collateral | Initial + variation margin |
| Liquidity | Variable | Generally liquid for major contracts |
| Examples | OTC FX forwards, bespoke commodity | S&P 500 futures, oil futures |

### Swaps

A **swap** is an agreement to exchange cash flows over time. Most common:

**Interest rate swap.** Exchange floating for fixed payments on a notional.
- 'Vanilla' interest rate swap: pay fixed, receive floating (or vice versa).

**Currency swap.** Exchange principal and interest in different currencies.

**Equity swap.** Exchange equity returns for fixed/floating.

**Commodity swap.** Exchange floating commodity price for fixed.

**Credit default swap (CDS).** Payment contingent on a credit event.

Swaps can be thought of as a series of forward contracts settled periodically.

### Options

**Call option.** Right to buy the underlying at a specified strike price by expiration.

**Put option.** Right to sell the underlying at a specified strike price by expiration.

**European option.** Exercise only at expiration.

**American option.** Exercise at any time before expiration.

**Option premium.** The price paid for the option (positive at initiation).

This is the key contrast with forwards/futures: options have **upfront cost** because of the asymmetric payoff.

### OTC vs exchange-traded

**Over-the-counter (OTC):**
- Bilateral contracts between two parties.
- Customised terms.
- Counterparty risk (each party relies on the other).
- Less regulated historically; more regulated post-2008.
- Examples: most forwards, swaps, exotic options.

**Exchange-traded:**
- Standardised contracts on a regulated exchange.
- Clearing house as central counterparty (CCP) — reduces counterparty risk.
- Daily settlement (mark-to-market).
- Margin requirements.
- More transparent pricing.
- Examples: futures, listed options on stocks/indices.

### Why derivatives exist

**Hedging.** Lock in prices/rates to reduce uncertainty.
- Airlines hedge fuel costs.
- Exporters hedge currency exposure.
- Pension funds hedge interest rate risk.

**Speculation.** Take directional bets with leverage.
- Hedge funds, prop trading.

**Arbitrage.** Profit from temporary price differences.
- Index arbitrage, basis trading.

**Information.** Derivatives reveal expectations.
- Futures prices show expected future spot.
- Option implied volatility shows expected risk.

**Leverage.** Get exposure with less capital.
- Notional vs margin can be 10:1, 100:1, or more.

**Customisation.** OTC derivatives let parties tailor specific risks.

### Risks of derivatives

**Market risk.** Underlying moves against you.

**Counterparty risk.** Counterparty defaults (mitigated for exchange-traded, mostly).

**Liquidity risk.** Hard to exit position at fair value.

**Operational risk.** Documentation, settlement, calculation errors.

**Model risk.** For complex derivatives, valuation depends on model assumptions.

**Systemic risk.** Concentrated positions can transmit shocks (2008).

### Regulatory context

Post-2008 reforms:
- Mandatory central clearing for standardised OTC derivatives.
- Trade reporting requirements.
- Higher capital for non-cleared OTC.
- Position limits in some markets.

Key regulators:
- US: SEC (securities), CFTC (commodities/futures).
- EU: ESMA, EMIR rules.
- Other: country-specific authorities.

### Why this matters

Derivatives are huge — notional exposure across all derivatives exceeds $600 trillion globally. Most institutional portfolios use derivatives for hedging or efficient exposure. Understanding their structure is essential for risk management and CFA exam questions.
modes.pro:
## Derivatives at speed

### Definition

A derivative = financial contract whose value depends on an underlying (stock, bond, commodity, rate, index, credit event).

### Basic features

- **Underlying**: reference asset/rate/index
- **Notional**: size for payoff calc (rarely exchanged)
- **Counterparties**: long and short
- **Expiration**: maturity date
- **Payoff rule**: at expiration (and intermediate for some)
- **Initial value**: typically zero (except options pay premium)

### Two main families

**Forward commitments** (obligation to transact):
- Forwards (OTC, customised)
- Futures (exchange, standardised)
- Swaps (series of forwards)

**Contingent claims** (right, not obligation):
- Options (calls and puts)
- Credit default swaps

### Forwards vs futures

| | Forwards | Futures |
|---|---|---|
| Market | OTC | Exchange |
| Terms | Bespoke | Standard |
| Counterparty risk | High | Low (CCP) |
| Settlement | At maturity | Daily MTM |
| Margin | Bilateral collateral | Initial + variation |

### Swap types

- Interest rate (most common): pay fixed, receive floating
- Currency: exchange currencies + interest
- Equity: exchange equity returns for fixed/float
- Commodity: floating commodity for fixed
- Credit (CDS): contingent on credit event

### Options

- **Call**: right to buy at strike
- **Put**: right to sell at strike
- **European**: exercise only at expiry
- **American**: exercise anytime before expiry
- **Premium**: option price (positive at initiation)

### OTC vs exchange-traded

**OTC:**
- Customised, counterparty risk
- Less liquid historically
- Mostly forwards, swaps, exotic options

**Exchange-traded:**
- Standardised, CCP guarantees
- Daily margin
- Mostly futures, listed options

### Uses

- **Hedging**: reduce uncertainty
- **Speculation**: leveraged directional
- **Arbitrage**: exploit pricing differences
- **Leverage**: large exposure, small capital
- **Customisation**: bespoke risk transfer

### Risks

- Market, counterparty, liquidity, operational, model, systemic

### Post-2008 reforms

- Central clearing for standardised OTC
- Trade reporting
- Higher capital for non-cleared OTC

examples.title: OTC forward vs exchange-traded future
examples.body:
**Scenario.** UK importer needs to buy $5m of USD in 6 months for inventory.

**Option 1: OTC forward.**
- Calls bank, agrees to buy $5m at GBP/USD = 1.25.
- No money exchanged today.
- At 6 months, hands over £4m, receives $5m.
- **Risks**: bank could fail; rate at maturity is fixed regardless.

**Option 2: Exchange-traded futures.**
- Buys GBP/USD futures contracts standardised at $125,000 each → buys 40 contracts.
- Posts initial margin (say $5,000 per contract = $200,000).
- Daily variation margin paid/received as rate moves.
- At 6 months, closes positions or takes delivery (rarely).
- **Risks**: needs to manage daily margin; basis risk (futures expiry may not match exact need date).

**Trade-off**: forward is convenient and exact; futures are transparent and have low counterparty risk but require margin operations.

**Typical choice for corporates**: forwards. **For traders/hedge funds**: futures.

pitfalls: **Confusing notional with market value.** Notional is the size of the contract; the actual P&L is often much smaller.
**Underestimating counterparty risk in OTC derivatives.** Pre-2008, this was a massive oversight (Lehman, AIG).
**Treating derivatives as 'risky' without understanding the hedging context.** Derivatives can reduce or increase risk depending on use.
**Forgetting daily margin requirements for futures.** Margin calls can force liquidation even if your view is correct long-term.

faq.q: Why is the world derivative notional so huge ($600+ trillion)?
faq.a:
**It's the gross sum of all outstanding contract sizes**, but notional dramatically overstates actual economic exposure.

**Why notional is so large:**
- Each interest rate swap covers a large principal but P&L is on the rate difference.
- Many positions offset each other (Bank A long $1bn with Bank B; Bank B long $1bn with Bank C, etc.).
- New contracts continually issued; notional accumulates.

**Net economic exposure** (gross market value or net potential loss) is far smaller — typically <5% of notional. Globally that's still tens of trillions, but much less alarming than $600T.

**The point of the metric**: notional is a proxy for activity and complexity, not actual risk. Market value or value-at-risk are better measures of actual exposure.
